name: Woody Guthrie
note: Dylan used the melody of Guthrie’s “1913 Massacre” for “Song to Woody,” his tribute to the older songwriter.

name: Buddy Holly
note: In his Nobel lecture Dylan recalls seeing Holly onstage as a teenager. He remembered the eye contact as vividly as the music.

name: Lead Belly
note: Dylan describes receiving a Lead Belly record after seeing Buddy Holly. It introduced him to a repertoire he set out to learn.

name: Odetta
note: Hearing Odetta sing and play guitar helped turn the teenage Dylan toward folk music. He learned songs from her records.

name: Robert Johnson
note: Johnson’s recordings became a touchstone for Dylan, who described their effect on him in Chronicles.

name: Little Richard
note: Dylan remembered Little Richard as an early model for his own performing life. His high-school yearbook even named joining Richard as his ambition.

name: Martin Carthy
note: Carthy played “Scarborough Fair” for Dylan during his first visit to England. Its melodic shape can be heard in “Girl from the North Country.”

name: Dave Van Ronk
note: Dylan learned Van Ronk’s arrangement of “House of the Rising Sun” and recorded it on his debut album.

name: The Beatles
note: John Lennon identified “You’ve Got to Hide Your Love Away” with his Dylan period. Listen to the acoustic arrangement and the first-person lyric.

name: Bruce Springsteen
note: Introducing Dylan at the Rock Hall, Springsteen recalled the opening snare hit of “Like a Rolling Stone” and the possibilities it opened for him as a listener.

name: Patti Smith
note: Smith described her attachment to Dylan’s writing in her account of singing “A Hard Rain’s A-Gonna Fall” at the Nobel ceremony.

name: The Byrds
note: Roger McGuinn turned “Mr. Tambourine Man” into a compact electric single. His twelve-string guitar became central to the Byrds’ sound.

name: Jimi Hendrix
note: Hendrix rebuilt “All Along the Watchtower” around electric guitar. Dylan in turn drew on that arrangement in his live performances.

name: Lucinda Williams
note: Williams has described Dylan as a songwriting influence. Her interpretations include a whole album of his songs, Lu’s Jukebox Vol. 3.

name: David Bowie
note: Bowie addressed Dylan directly in “Song for Bob Dylan,” recorded for Hunky Dory.

name: The Band
note: Playing with Dylan on tour and making the Basement Tapes gave the musicians who became the Band a shared body of songs and arrangements.
